key_terms.meaning: The time slot, in seconds, that one channel symbol occupies; consecutive symbols are sent T apart.
Symbols per second, Rₛ = 1/T, measured in baud; for binary signalling it equals the bit rate.
The smallest channel bandwidth that carries Rₛ symbols/s with zero ISI, equal to Rₛ/2 = 1/(2T) hertz.
Zero ISI at the sampling instants needs h(0) = 1 and h(kT) = 0 for every nonzero integer k; in frequency, Σₙ H(f − n/T) = T for |f| ≤ 1/(2T).
D = (1/|h(0)|)·Σ_{k≠0} |h(kT)|, the worst-case fraction of the wanted sample spoiled by all neighbouring pulses.
A Nyquist pulse shape with a cosinusoidal roll-off of factor α (0 ≤ α ≤ 1) whose bandwidth is (1+α)/(2T) hertz.
The fraction of extra bandwidth used beyond the Nyquist minimum; excess bandwidth = α·Rₛ/2 hertz.
The overlay of many symbol-length received segments on an oscilloscope; the eye opening shows noise margin and ISI, the crossing width shows timing-jitter tolerance.
A tapped delay line whose frequency response is the exact inverse of the channel, so ISI is forced to zero at the sampling instants.
An equalizer whose tap weights update themselves from the received data, usually by the LMS algorithm, to track a changing channel.
One of a set of orthonormal waveforms φᵢ(t) of energy 1 that are used as coordinate axes for a signal set.
A step-by-step construction that turns any set of M signals into an orthonormal basis of at most M dimensions.
The receive filter h(t) = s(T − t), the signal time-reversed and shifted by T; it gives the largest output SNR at the sampling instant.
A multiplier that forms r(t)·s(t) followed by an integrate-and-dump over 0 to T; it produces the same sample value as the matched filter.
Additive white Gaussian noise: a random waveform with flat power spectral density N₀/2 (two-sided) and Gaussian amplitude at every instant.
Q(x) = (1/√(2π))∫ₓ^∞ e^(−u²/2) du, the tail probability of a unit Gaussian; used as the standard form of P(e).
The part of signal space whose received points are decided in favour of a particular signal; for AWGN these regions are separated by perpendicular bisectors.
The smallest Euclidean distance between any two signal points; the error probability falls as Q(d_min/√(2N₀)).
A deliberate, known one-symbol ISI created by a 1 + D filter so a binary stream can be sent in the Nyquist bandwidth Rₛ/2; the received levels become three.
Pulse amplitude modulation with M equally spaced levels, each symbol carrying log₂M bits.
The bandwidth used above the Nyquist minimum, equal to α·Rₛ/2 hertz for a raised-cosine pulse.

takeaways: Intersymbol interference is the spill of neighbouring pulses into the current sample; it is measured by the sampled values h(kT) of the overall pulse.
Nyquist's criterion h(kT) = 0 for k ≠ 0 is the exact condition for zero ISI, and it fixes the minimum bandwidth at half the symbol rate.
A raised-cosine pulse meets Nyquist's condition with a gradual, realisable spectrum, trading α·Rₛ/2 hertz of excess bandwidth for easier filters and a wider eye.
The eye pattern is the practical test of pulse shaping: its opening measures noise margin, its width measures timing-jitter tolerance.
A zero-forcing equalizer inverts the channel exactly but boosts noise where the channel is weak; an adaptive LMS equalizer trades a little residual ISI for stability and tracking.
Gram-Schmidt shows that M signals of duration T live in at most M dimensions, so a receiver only needs those coordinates, not the whole waveform.
The matched filter and the correlation receiver give the same sample; the matched filter reaches the maximum SNR of 2E/N₀ at t = T.
In AWGN the optimum detector picks the nearest signal point, so P(e) depends only on the distances between points and on N₀.
M-ary PAM multiplies the bit rate by log₂M at the same symbol rate but needs more power per bit; the error probability expression carries both effects.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit almost always join three ideas — the Nyquist zero-ISI condition, a raised-cosine bandwidth design, and a matched-filter error-probability result — so keep the formulas for bandwidth, SNR and Q(·) at your fingertips.

bank.q: Define intersymbol interference. Derive the condition for zero ISI at the sampling instants and state Nyquist's criterion in both the time domain and the frequency domain.
outline: Received sample y(kT) = Σ aₙ h(kT − nT) + noise; all terms with n ≠ k are ISI
Zero ISI needs h(0) ≠ 0 and h(kT) = 0 for all k ≠ 0
Frequency-domain form: Σₙ H(f − n/T) = T for |f| ≤ 1/(2T)
Minimum bandwidth = 1/(2T) = Rₛ/2, the Nyquist bandwidth
Peak distortion D = Σ|h(kT)|/|h(0)| as the practical measure

bank.q: Explain how an eye pattern is generated and how noise margin, timing-jitter tolerance and the amount of ISI are read from it.
outline: Overlay of many symbol-length traces triggered at the symbol rate
Vertical eye opening gives noise margin
Horizontal crossing width gives timing-jitter tolerance
Closing of the eye at the optimum sampling instant indicates ISI
Slope of the eye at the crossing shows sensitivity to timing error

bank.q: Describe the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization procedure. Show that a set of M signals of duration T spans a space of at most M dimensions.
outline: Start with φ₁ = s₁/√E₁
Subtract projections of earlier basis functions, then normalize
Stop early if the residual is zero, so dimension ≤ M
Signal vector coefficients are the inner products sᵢⱼ = ∫sᵢ(t)φⱼ(t)dt
Energy equals the squared length of the vector (Parseval)

bank.q: Define the matched filter. Prove that it maximises the output signal-to-noise ratio at the sampling instant, and state that maximum.
outline: Take h(t) = s(T − t)
Output at T is the signal energy E; noise output variance is (N₀/2)·E
Cauchy-Schwarz inequality shows no other h(t) does better
Peak SNR = 2E/N₀ (real signals, two-sided PSD N₀/2)
Impulse response is the signal time-reversed and delayed by T, so the filter is unrealisable until T

bank.q: Explain correlative coding with the duobinary scheme. Why does a deliberately introduced ISI let a binary stream use only Rₛ/2 of bandwidth?
outline: Binary data through a 1 + D filter gives three received levels
Overall response is a Nyquist pulse plus a one-symbol delayed copy
Bandwidth used is Rₛ/2, the Nyquist minimum for the symbol rate
Received sample bₖ = aₖ + aₖ₋₁ is decoded by comparison with previous decisions or by precoding
Error propagation is avoided by differential precoding

bank.q: A binary baseband system sends 2400 symbols per second through a raised-cosine filter with roll-off α = 0.5. Find the symbol period, the Nyquist bandwidth, the absolute bandwidth and the excess bandwidth. Repeat for α = 0 and α = 1 and comment.
outline: Nyquist bandwidth = Rₛ/2 = 1200 Hz
Absolute bandwidth = (1+α)Rₛ/2 = 1800 Hz
Excess bandwidth = αRₛ/2 = 600 Hz
α = 0 gives an ideal brick-wall 1200 Hz; α = 1 gives 2400 Hz; larger α means easier filters but more bandwidth

bank.q: A channel has the sampled overall response h(0) = 0.8, h(T) = 0.3, h(−T) = 0.1, all other samples zero. Design a three-tap zero-forcing equalizer and find the residual ISI after equalization.
outline: Write the convolution of channel taps with equalizer taps
Set the equalized response to 1 at k = 0 and 0 at k = ±1
Solve the three linear equations for the tap weights
Residual ISI is zero at ±T but nonzero at other instants unless the equalizer is longer
Comment on noise enhancement from the inverse response

bank.q: A binary antipodal baseband system uses pulses of energy E_b and AWGN of two-sided density N₀/2. Find the error probability when E_b/N₀ = 10 (10 dB), and when it is 7 dB. Use Q(1) ≈ 0.159, Q(2) ≈ 0.0228, Q(3) ≈ 0.00135, Q(4) ≈ 3.2×10⁻⁵.
outline: 10 dB gives 2E_b/N₀ = 20, √20 ≈ 4.47, so P(e) is just below 3.2×10⁻⁵
7 dB gives 2E_b/N₀ ≈ 10.02, √ ≈ 3.17, so P(e) is about 8×10⁻⁴
Note the steep fall of Q(·) with SNR

bank.q: Four equally likely signals of duration T are given. Use Gram-Schmidt to build the basis, draw the signal space, find d_min, and write P(e) for optimum detection in AWGN with spectral density N₀/2.
outline: Compute energies and inner products
Normalize the first signal, project the rest, stop when residual is zero
State the dimension of the space
Place the points and read d_min from the geometry
For AWGN, P(e) ≈ N̄_min Q(d_min/√(2N₀)), with N̄_min the average number of nearest neighbours

bank.q: A 16-level PAM system sends data at 64 kbit/s over a baseband channel with a raised-cosine pulse of α = 0.25. Find the symbol rate, the number of levels used, the bandwidth needed, and compare the bandwidth with binary transmission at the same bit rate.
outline: log₂16 = 4 bits per symbol
Bandwidth = (1+α)Rₛ/2 = 1.25×8000 = 10 kHz
Binary at 64 kbit/s needs 40 kHz at the same α
Trade-off: four times less bandwidth but more power per bit for the same P(e)

bank.q: Compare a zero-forcing equalizer with an adaptive LMS equalizer. Discuss noise enhancement, residual ISI, convergence and behaviour on a time-varying channel.
outline: Zero-forcing inverts the channel exactly: ISI zero, but noise is amplified where |H(f)| is small
LMS minimises mean-square error, so it balances ISI against noise
Adaptive weights update as wₖ₊₁ = wₖ + μ·eₖ·rₖ; step size μ sets speed versus stability
Training sequence then decision-directed mode
Zero-forcing is simple but fragile; adaptive equalizers track a changing channel at the cost of convergence time

bank.q: A baseband link must carry a given bit rate through a channel of fixed bandwidth. Discuss how you would choose between binary and M-ary PAM and between small and large roll-off, and how the eye pattern and the error probability together decide the design.
outline: Bandwidth needed = (1+α)Rₛ/2 with Rₛ = R_b/log₂M
Larger M reduces bandwidth but raises required E_b/N₀
Larger α eases filter design and timing tolerance but uses more bandwidth
Eye opening tells the practical noise and jitter margin left
Final choice balances power, bandwidth and hardware cost; check P(e) against the target

bank.q: Explain why the matched filter is optimum in AWGN. Then evaluate the loss when the receiver filter is mismatched and when the sampling instant is off by a fraction of T.
outline: Matched filter maximises SNR by the Cauchy-Schwarz bound; equality only for h(t) ∝ s(T − t)
Mismatch reduces output SNR in proportion to the squared normalized correlation
Timing error reduces the wanted sample and adds ISI from neighbours
Eye pattern width quantifies the tolerable timing error
Practical receivers use a timing-recovery loop to hold the sampling instant near the eye centre

bank.q: Derive the symbol error probability of M-ary PAM in AWGN and discuss the power penalty as M grows. Why is the penalty stated per bit rather than per symbol?
outline: Levels spaced 2d apart, average energy Eₛ = (M²−1)d²/3
Substitute Eₛ = E_b log₂M to get the per-bit form
Each doubling of M costs roughly 4 to 5 dB in E_b/N₀ at high M
Per-bit comparison is fair because the same data is sent in less bandwidth

glossary.def: The contamination of one symbol's sample by the tails of pulses belonging to other symbols.
Half the symbol rate, 1/(2T) hertz, the least bandwidth in which zero-ISI signalling is possible.
One symbol per second; the unit of symbol rate Rₛ = 1/T.
Any pulse shape whose sampled values are 1 at the centre and exactly 0 at every other symbol instant.
The pulse sin(πt/T)/(πt/T); it is the ideal Nyquist pulse but needs infinite delay and a brick-wall spectrum.
The parameter α between 0 and 1 that fixes how much extra bandwidth a raised-cosine pulse uses.
The bandwidth used beyond the Nyquist minimum, equal to αRₛ/2 hertz.
A display formed by overlaying received symbol-length segments, whose opening shows the margin against noise and ISI.
A filter, usually a tapped delay line, placed at the receiver to cancel the ISI introduced by the channel.
An equalizer that makes the overall sampled response exactly 1 at the centre and 0 at all other symbol instants.
The least-mean-square update wₖ₊₁ = wₖ + μ·eₖ·rₖ that adapts equalizer taps from the error between the received and decided symbol.
A geometric view in which each signal of duration T is a point whose coordinates are its projections on the basis functions.
A set of waveforms of unit energy that are mutually orthogonal, used as the axes of the signal space.
A constructive method that produces an orthonormal basis from any set of signals by subtracting projections.
The filter whose impulse response is the signal reversed in time and delayed by the symbol period, giving maximum output SNR.
A multiplier followed by an integrate-and-dump that computes the inner product of the received signal with a reference signal.
A channel that adds white Gaussian noise of flat spectral density to the transmitted signal.
The Gaussian tail probability Q(x); every error probability in this unit is written in terms of it.
The set of received points that the detector maps to one particular transmitted signal.
The smallest separation between two signal points; it sets the error probability in AWGN.
Signalling that deliberately adds a known, controlled ISI so that the spectrum fits a realisable Nyquist filter.
A correlative scheme using a 1 + D response that sends binary data in the Nyquist bandwidth with three received levels.
Pulse amplitude modulation with M levels, carrying log₂M bits per symbol.
Random variation of the sampling instant about the ideal point, which reduces the eye opening.
